analysis.one_liner: Counts military and veterans' education benefits against the federal revenue cap on for-profit colleges.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees and three subcommittees, never received a vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill closed a loophole in the "90/10 rule," which says for-profit colleges must get at least 10% of their revenue from sources other than federal student aid or lose access to federal aid programs. Under current law, GI Bill benefits, military tuition assistance, and other veterans' education money count toward that 10% — meaning a school could actually collect nearly all of its revenue from the federal government and still qualify. This bill would have counted military and veterans' benefits as federal revenue, so schools that lived almost entirely off service members' education benefits would lose eligibility for federal student aid and for the education programs run by the Defense Department and the VA.
analysis.who_benefits: Service members, veterans, and their families who use GI Bill and military tuition benefits would be protected from for-profit colleges that set up shop near military bases and collect most of their revenue from federal education benefits while providing little educational value in return. Taxpayers also benefit, since federal money would stop flowing to schools that fail the revenue test.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Service members and veterans using education benefits

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Higher Education Act so that the existing '90/10 rule' counts revenue from military and veteran education programs — GI Bill benefits under title 38, Defense Department tuition assistance under title 10, and related programs — toward the 90% cap on federal revenue, instead of letting schools count them as private revenue.

It requires the Secretaries of Defense and Veterans Affairs to enforce any ineligibility determination against all federal education programs they administer, and to publish on their websites the name of the offending school, how it failed, and how long it is barred.

It sets a minimum two-year penalty: a for-profit school that misses the requirement for two consecutive years loses access to all federal educational assistance, and must demonstrate two additional years of compliance to regain eligibility.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit colleges that depend on military and veteran education benefits for a large share of their revenue: they would lose federal student aid eligibility and access to DoD and VA education programs if they failed the revenue test for two consecutive years.
analysis.who_pays_short: For-profit colleges reliant on GI Bill money

drawbacks.text: For-profit colleges argued that counting military and veteran benefits in the 90/10 calculation could cut off schools that mainly serve service members, forcing closures that would interrupt students mid-program.

The two-year ineligibility penalty is triggered after just two consecutive years of noncompliance, and regaining eligibility itself requires two more years of demonstrated compliance — a punishment some would call heavy-handed even for poorly performing schools.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: service members and veterans would be far less likely to have their education benefits consumed by low-quality for-profit programs, because schools that rely on federal military and veteran dollars for most of their revenue would face real consequences. The costs are narrow: schools that truly depend on military tuition dollars would have to diversify or exit, and an honest supporter would acknowledge that enforcement could disrupt enrollments for students mid-program, though the bill requires public notice of which schools are affected so students can choose elsewhere.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to three House committees, then parked in three subcommittees, and none of them ever advanced it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Jackie Speier introduced the bill on November 5, 2015, with 22 original cosponsors plus 3 more, for a total of 25 (24 Democrats, 1 Republican).
The House referred it to the Education and the Workforce, Armed Services, and Veterans' Affairs committees on the day it was introduced.

Between November and March 2016 it was passed down to three subcommittees — Military Personnel, Economic Opportunity, and Higher Education and Workforce Training — and no further action was ever taken.
It never received a markup or a floor vote in either chamber, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges that collect GI Bill and military tuition dollars kept a rule that lets those benefits count as private revenue, so they can draw up to 90% of their revenue from federal sources. Students and service members gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: For-profit colleges relying on GI Bill revenue

against.what_they_did: The bill sat in the Subcommittee on Higher Education and Workforce Training from March 2016 onward with no markup and no vote.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic — 24 of the 25 cosponsors — with a single Republican, Rep. Walter Jones of North Carolina, and no Republican committee action ever advanced the bill.

industries.note: The bill closes a loophole that lets for-profit schools count GI Bill and military tuition assistance as non-federal revenue, so schools could no longer get up to 90% of their revenue from federal military and veteran benefits plus federal student aid. It also adds mandatory two-year penalties and public disclosure. These schools' revenue model depends heavily on taxpayer-funded tuition; the bill's interests run against the bill's protections for service members and veterans.
Public and nonprofit colleges are not proprietary institutions and were not covered by the 90/10 rule; no direct effect.

industries.industry: Defense Department and VA contractors and vendors in military education
industries.note: Businesses built around servicing military education benefits at for-profit campuses would lose access when a school is declared ineligible, since DoD and VA benefits could no longer be used there.
